content: 1. Vitamin A supplementation is not recommended as a public health intervention for reducing infant morbidity and mortality in infants aged 1–5 months. This recommendation is based on moderate-quality evidence for infant mortality outcomes and low-quality evidence for other critical outcomes, including the side effect of bulging fontanelles. 2. In settings where vitamin A deficiency is a public health problem, vitamin A supplementation is recommended for infants and children aged 6–59 months to reduce child morbidity and mortality. This recommendation is supported by high-quality evidence for all-cause mortality and moderate-to-very low-quality evidence for other critical outcomes. For HIV-positive children, moderate-quality evidence supports the reduction of all-cause mortality. 3. Daily iron supplementation is recommended as a public health intervention for infants and young children aged 6–23 months living in areas with high anemia prevalence. This intervention aims to prevent iron deficiency and anemia, with a suggested dosage of 5 mg of elemental iron daily for three consecutive months each year. The recommendation is based on moderate-quality evidence. 4. For preschool-age children aged 24–59 months in areas with high anemia prevalence, daily iron supplementation is recommended to increase hemoglobin concentrations and improve iron status. The suggested dosage is 30 mg of elemental iron daily for three consecutive months each year. This recommendation is supported by very low-quality evidence. 5. School-age children aged 60 months and older living in areas with high anemia prevalence should receive daily iron supplementation to prevent iron deficiency and anemia. The suggested dosage is 30–60 mg of elemental iron daily for three consecutive months each year. This recommendation is based on high-quality evidence. 6. In malaria-endemic areas, iron supplementation for infants and children should be provided alongside public health measures to prevent, diagnose, and treat malaria. This recommendation is supported by high-quality evidence. 7. In populations where anemia is a public health problem, point-of-use fortification of complementary foods with iron-containing micronutrient powders is recommended for infants and young children aged 6–23 months to improve iron status and reduce anemia. The suggested regimen includes 5 mg of elemental iron, 300 µg of retinol (vitamin A), and 5 mg of elemental zinc, with or without other micronutrients, to achieve 100% of the recommended nutrient intake. The program target is 90 sachets over a six-month period. This recommendation is based on moderate-quality evidence. 8. For children aged 2–12 years in populations where anemia is a public health problem, point-of-use fortification of foods with iron-containing micronutrient powders is recommended to improve iron status and reduce anemia. The suggested dosage ranges from 5 to 30 mg of elemental iron, along with 300 µg of retinol (vitamin A) and 5 mg of elemental zinc, with or without other micronutrients. The program target is 90 sachets over a six-month period. This recommendation is supported by moderate-quality evidence. 9. Infants born to mothers with suspected, probable, or confirmed Zika virus infection, or who reside in or have traveled to areas of ongoing Zika virus transmission, should be fed according to standard infant feeding guidelines. Breastfeeding should begin within one hour of birth, be exclusive for six months, and continue alongside the timely introduction of safe and adequate complementary foods up to two years of age or beyond. 10. In areas of moderate-to-high malaria transmission in Africa, where sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) remains effective, intermittent preventive treatment with SP should be provided to infants at the time of the second and third rounds of diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis (DTP) vaccination and measles vaccination. This is a strong recommendation. 11. In areas with highly seasonal malaria transmission in the sub-Sahel region of Africa, seasonal malaria chemoprevention with monthly amodiaquine plus SP is recommended for all children under six years of age during each transmission season. This recommendation is supported by high-quality evidence. 12. In settings where tuberculosis (TB) is highly endemic or there is a high risk of exposure, a single dose of the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine should be given to all infants. However, BCG vaccination should not be given to children known to be HIV-infected. For infants with unknown HIV status born to HIV-positive mothers, BCG vaccination should be considered based on local factors. 13. Clinical evaluation of household and close contacts of TB cases should prioritize children with TB symptoms, children under five years of age, children with immunocompromising conditions (especially those living with HIV), and child contacts of multidrug-resistant or extensively drug-resistant TB cases. This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 14. Children under five years of age who are household or close contacts of TB cases and are found not to have active TB after clinical evaluation should receive six months of isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) at a dosage of 10 mg/kg per day (range 7–15 mg/kg, maximum dose 300 mg/day). This recommendation is supported by high-quality evidence. 15. In settings with high HIV prevalence, all household and close contacts of TB cases should be counseled and tested for HIV. In low HIV prevalence settings, household members and close contacts of TB cases with symptoms compatible with TB disease may be offered HIV counseling and testing as part of their clinical evaluation. 16. Infants born to mothers with HIV who are at high risk of acquiring HIV should receive dual prophylaxis with zidovudine (AZT) and nevirapine (NVP) for the first six weeks of life, regardless of feeding method. Breastfed infants at high risk of acquiring HIV should continue prophylaxis for an additional six weeks, using either AZT and NVP or NVP alone. 17. Mothers known to be HIV-infected should exclusively breastfeed their infants for the first six months of life, introducing appropriate complementary foods thereafter. Breastfeeding should continue for at least 12 months and may extend up to 24 months or longer while ensuring adherence to antiretroviral therapy (ART). Breastfeeding should only stop once a nutritionally adequate and safe diet without breast milk can be provided. 18. Mothers living with HIV who decide to stop breastfeeding should do so gradually within one month. ARV prophylaxis for mothers or infants should continue for one week after breastfeeding cessation. Abrupt cessation of breastfeeding is not advisable.
